title: LSA Act s. 19 — Organization of Lok Adalats (LSA Act s. 19)

content.overview: Section 19 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 is the organisation provision for Lok Adalats. A State or District Authority, the Supreme Court or High Court Legal Services Committee, or a Taluk Legal Services Committee may organise Lok Adalats at intervals and places, and for areas and jurisdiction, as it thinks fit. A Lok Adalat consists of serving or retired judicial officers and other persons of the area, as specified by the organising body. It may determine and arrive at a compromise or settlement in a case pending before, or a matter falling within the jurisdiction of and not yet brought before, the court for which it is organised. It has no jurisdiction over an offence that is not compoundable.

learningObjectives: Identify who may organise a Lok Adalat under s. 19 and how its composition is specified.
State the pending-case and pre-litigation jurisdiction in s. 19(5).
Apply the proviso that a Lok Adalat has no jurisdiction over a non-compoundable offence.
enhancement.definition: Section 19 authorises specified legal services authorities and committees to organise Lok Adalats, fixes their composition, and defines the compromise or settlement jurisdiction, excluding non-compoundable offences.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A Lok Adalat is a statutorily organised settlement forum. Its jurisdiction is to arrive at a compromise or settlement, not to try a non-compoundable offence, and an award follows only if settlement is reached.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s. 19; cognizance in s. 20; award in s. 21; Permanent Lok Adalat establishment is a separate non-obstante regime under s. 22B.
essentialIngredients: Organising authority identified (State/District Authority, SCLSC, HCLSC, or Taluk Committee)
Area, interval and jurisdiction specified by that body
Composition: serving or retired judicial officers and other persons of the area
Dispute is a pending case or a matter within the court's jurisdiction not yet filed
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 19(1) is an enabling organisation power, not a power to decide a dispute on merits. Subsection (2) requires a mix of judicial officers and other persons, specified by the organising authority. Subsection (5) covers both referred pending cases and pre-litigation matters falling within the jurisdiction of the court for which the Lok Adalat is organised. The proviso is a hard jurisdictional limit: no case or matter relating to an offence not compoundable under any law. Settlement jurisdiction under s. 19 must be separated from Permanent Lok Adalat establishment under s. 22B, which is notwithstanding s. 19 and is confined to notified public utility services.
examples: A District Authority organises a Lok Adalat for pending money suits in that district court.
Parties seek a pre-litigation settlement of a civil claim that could have been filed in the court for which the Lok Adalat is organised.
A prosecution for a non-compoundable offence is placed before the Lok Adalat; s. 19(5) proviso excludes jurisdiction.
enhancement.problemApplication: Name the organising body and area; classify the dispute as pending or pre-litigation; test compoundability if criminal; only then move to s. 20 reference and s. 21 effect. Do not treat organisation under s. 19 as itself an award.

keyTakeaways: Section 19 organises the Lok Adalat; it does not itself make the award.
Composition is judicial officers plus other persons specified by the organiser.
Jurisdiction covers pending cases and eligible pre-litigation matters.
